title: Look beyond old climate fault lines / Three steps COP should take for tangible outcomes
where: Editorial page, page 10 (editorial) and Ideas page, page 11 (Sumit Prasad, CEEW)
syllabus: GS3 › Conservation, environmental degradation (climate change, UNFCCC) · GS2 › Important international institutions and fora; India and the Global South · GS4 › Environmental ethics; climate justice
summary: Ahead of COP31 in Antalya, India has not committed to the '35 by 35' global electrification target, citing sovereignty and poverty eradication; the CEEW asks the 'COP of implementation' to show reports, finance and a scorecard.
evolution: First Loss and Damage payout goes to Nepal: climate justice needs quicker compensation.
Energy security depends on whether and how India electrifies (electrification thread).
ideas: National circumstances first: India is yet to back the '35 by 35' target (raise electricity's share of global energy use from 23% in 2023 to 35% by 2035), saying every country must weigh sovereignty and poverty eradication; developing countries face weaker grids and stressed utilities.
GS3 · Climate change / GS2 · India's stand in climate fora
India resists one-size targets like '35 by 35' because weak grids and poverty make national circumstances decisive.

An unfair critique: India is among a small group making steady progress on Paris commitments; calling its early delivery a sign of low ambition ignores bottlenecks in developed countries and the Global North's failure on finance and technology.
GS3 · Paris Agreement / climate justice
India's early delivery on Paris targets shows good faith, while the North's finance shortfall remains the real ambition gap.

Climate action is in India's own interest: greater urgency serves its development and strategy, and lets it lead the Global South through the International Solar Alliance and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure.
GS2 · India-led institutions / Global South
Through the ISA and CDRI, India can turn climate action into leadership of the Global South.

'Implementation COP' risks becoming a slogan: claimed at COP27, COP30 and COP31; 2035 NDCs were due in February 2025 and second transparency reports by December 31, yet by late October only Colombia and Turkey had filed.
GS2 · UNFCCC process
A COP can claim to be about implementation only if parties report on time; by late October only two had filed transparency reports.

Three steps for credibility: every party files its transparency report on time; developed countries report finance delivered and promised; the presidency publishes an annual scorecard for its voluntary 2035 targets and Climate Implementation Bridge.
GS2 · Global governance / GS3 · Climate finance
Scorecards for voluntary pledges and reports on delivered finance would turn COP summits from promises into accountability.
keywords: Biennial Transparency Report (BTR)
Report under the Paris Agreement on emissions and progress against NDCs
GS3 · Climate governance
Timely Biennial Transparency Reports are the evidence an 'implementation COP' needs.
Action Agenda
The voluntary, non-negotiated track where presidencies rally pledges from states and non-state actors
GS2 · Climate diplomacy
The Action Agenda gains traction fast but delivers little without a scorecard.
National circumstances
Paris principle that each country's targets reflect its capacities and development needs
GS3 · Climate justice
India cites national circumstances to keep its sovereign right to set its own energy mix.
Electrification
Shifting energy use from fuels to electricity, e.g. EVs and electric heating
GS3 · Energy transition
Electrification helps decarbonise only when the grid itself is clean and reliable.
Climate finance credibility
Whether developed countries deliver the money they promise
GS3 · Climate finance / GS2
For developing countries, climate finance delivered, not pledged, is the barometer of global good faith.
data: Cooperative climate initiatives launched since 2015 that have met their goals
Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW)
Only about 5% of 203 cooperative climate initiatives since 2015 met their goals (CEEW): pledges outrun delivery.
Electricity's share of global energy use in 2023, and the '35 by 35' target for 2035
COP31 co-presidencies' proposal (Turkey and Australia), via IE
COP31's '35 by 35' plan would raise electricity's share of global energy use from 23% to 35% by 2035.
examples: International Solar Alliance and CDRI
India-led institutions that can anchor Global South leadership
GS2 · International institutions · GS3 · Climate
The ISA and CDRI give India institutional tools to lead climate action for the Global South.
Turkey files its transparency report early
Host country sets an example before COP31
GS4
GS2 · Climate diplomacy · GS4 · Leading by example
Turkey filing its BTR early shows that a presidency's credibility comes from doing first what it asks of others.
Turkey–Australia shared presidency
Turkey hosts and leads the Action Agenda; Australia steers negotiations
GS2 · Global governance
The COP31 split between Turkey and Australia shows compromise solving a hosting deadlock.
pyqs: Review of India's Paris commitments, how COP26 strengthened them, and the first NDC.
'Clean energy is the order of the day': India's changing climate policy in international fora.
Major outcomes of COP26 and India's commitments.
Purpose of the Green Grid Initiative at COP26 and its origin in the ISA.
Carbon credits and CDM under the UNFCCC despite the slide in their value.
How India, its Himalayan and coastal states will be affected by climate change.

trend.t: Climate questions moved from mechanisms (carbon credits and CDM, 2014) and impacts on India (2017) to COP outcomes and India's commitments (COP26 and the Green Grid, 2021), India's stance in international fora (2022) and a review of Paris commitments and NDCs (2025).
trend.watch: COPs and the Paris Agreement were asked in 2021, 2022 and 2025, so they are a must-study area. Questions ask what a COP decided, what India committed and how India positions itself, so track NDCs, finance and India-led initiatives.
focus: India's NDCs and progress (non-fossil capacity, emissions intensity, net zero 2070)
Climate finance and transparency under the Paris Agreement
India-led initiatives: ISA, CDRI, Green Grid

potential: "Climate summits have shifted from negotiation to implementation, but delivery lags." Discuss the challenges in making COPs deliver and the role India can play. (15 marks)
Should India accept global sectoral targets such as raising electricity's share in energy use? Examine with reference to national circumstances. (10 marks)
How can India use the International Solar Alliance and CDRI to lead the Global South on climate action? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Climate summits have shifted from negotiation to implementation, but delivery lags." Discuss the challenges in making COPs deliver and the role India can play.

answer.t: Turkey has branded COP31 in Antalya the 'COP of Implementation', a label also claimed at COP27 and COP30, yet only about 5% of 203 cooperative climate initiatives since 2015 have met their goals (CEEW).

pts.t: Many parties have not submitted their 2035 NDCs, though they were due in February 2025.
Second Biennial Transparency Reports are due by December 31, but few have been filed.
pts.ex: By late October only Colombia and Turkey had filed.

pts.t: Developed countries have repeatedly missed finance and technology commitments, eroding trust.
pts.ex: The $100 billion goal was met only years late.

pts.t: Action Agenda pledges are consensus-free and unenforced.
UNFCCC forums share progress but none enforces delivery.
The North presses the South on NDCs while the South sees scrutiny shifted from the North's own record.
India is among few countries making steady progress on Paris commitments.
pts.ex: 50% non-fossil installed capacity reached in 2025, five years early.

pts.t: India defends each country's right to set its energy mix and development path.
India can press for finance delivered, not promised.
India-led bodies can turn plans into projects.
Timely reporting strengthens India's moral authority to demand the same of others.
Lifestyle and resilience ideas suited to developing countries.
Anchor COP discussions in synthesis reports of NDCs and BTRs.
Developed countries to file biennial communications on finance delivered and promised.
Annual progress reports on voluntary targets.
Convert national priorities into investable projects.
Affordable access to storage, grids and clean technologies.
Equal weight to adaptation for vulnerable states.

answer.t: A COP's success must be measured by what the crisis demands; India can make 'implementation' mean delivered emissions cuts and delivered finance.

title: An alliance for multilateralism by other means
syllabus: GS2 › Important international institutions, agencies and fora: their structure and mandate; Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations; Environmental ethics
summary: The Partners for Multilateralism (P4M), launched at the 81st UNGA week and co-sponsored by India among others, commits to strengthening multilateral cooperation; the author argues it needs a concrete plan, clear principles and public engagement to succeed.
evolution: BRICS Parliamentary Forum seeks UNSC reform.
P4M, co-sponsored by India, pledges to strengthen multilateral cooperation.
ideas: Multilateralism under severe pressure: the US, a principal founder and long-time guarantor of the system, is rejecting it in word and deed, and other major players flout rules with impunity.
GS2 · International institutions
With the system's own guarantor walking away, middle and smaller powers must carry multilateralism.
A bridge across divides: co-sponsored by Australia, Brazil, Barbados, Canada, the EU, India and Kenya and signed by 18 more, P4M joins large and small countries of the Global South and North.
GS2 · Groupings involving India
P4M's mixed membership makes it a rare bridge between the Global North and South.

Reform language reflects a power shift: its pledge of cooperation that is 'open, fair, equitable, inclusive' echoes the South's long demand, now heard in a North weakened by Western turmoil and Transatlantic strain.
GS2 · Global order / Global South
The North's new receptiveness to reform reflects the Global South's growing clout and the West's own turmoil.
Plan and principles, or failure: P4M needs an action plan with costs and how they are shared, and clear principles that set it apart from efforts such as China's four Global Initiatives.
GS2 · Effect of policies of other countries
Coalitions without costed plans and clear principles join the list of well-intended but failed initiatives.
Engage people and the planet: reform drives fail when they ignore affected populations; P4M's diversity could offer ideas on deep ecology and interspecies coexistence for a new framework.
GS2 · Global governance / GS4 · Environmental ethics
Multilateralism will regain legitimacy only when it engages the public and protects the planet, not just states.
keywords: Minilateralism / coalition of the willing
Small, flexible groups of like-minded states acting where universal bodies stall
GS2 · Groupings
When universal institutions stall, coalitions of the willing like P4M keep cooperation alive.
Rules-based order
An international system governed by agreed norms rather than power
GS2 · International order
P4M's commitment to institutions and rule of law defends the rules-based order.
Reformed multilateralism
India's call to update global institutions to reflect today's realities
GS2 · India's foreign policy
India's co-sponsorship of P4M fits its long call for reformed multilateralism.
Bridging power
A country able to connect rival blocs
GS2 · India's global role
India's presence in P4M, BRICS and the Quad shows its role as a bridging power.
Deep ecology
A view that nature has value in itself, not only for human use
GS4 · Environmental ethics
Deep ecology asks global institutions to protect the planet for its own sake.
examples: Partners for Multilateralism (P4M)
Launched at the 81st UNGA week, co-sponsored by India
GS2 · International institutions · groupings · Essay
P4M shows middle powers trying to save multilateralism as the great powers turn away from it.
US rejection of the system it built
A founder and guarantor turning away
GS2 · Global order · Essay
The US turning against institutions it founded shows that even the architects of an order can abandon it.
China's four Global Initiatives
Rival visions of global governance
GS2 · India–China · global order
China's Global Initiatives show the contest over who will write the next rules of global governance.
pyqs: Unresolved UN reform amid East–West imbalance and the US vs Russo-Chinese entanglement.
BRICS as a counterweight in global governance amplifying the Global South.
Challenges as the world moves from free trade and multilateralism to protectionism and bilateralism.
Key areas of WTO reform amid trade war, keeping India's interests in mind.
Has India's image as leader of the marginalised nations faded in the new global order?
Waning globalisation and the rise of sovereign nationalism.

trend.t: Questions moved from the mandates of specific bodies (WTO, Bretton Woods, UNESCO, 2013–2019) to the crisis of the system itself: WTO reform amid trade war (2018), unresolved UN reform and great-power rivalry (2025), the retreat from multilateralism (2025) and BRICS as a voice of the Global South (2026).
trend.watch: Since 2025 UPSC asks about the crisis of multilateralism almost every year. Prepare why the order is weakening, who is reshaping it and India's role as a bridge for the Global South.
focus: Crisis of multilateralism and great-power retreat
Reform of the UN, WTO and other institutions

potential: "Multilateralism is under severe pressure, yet new coalitions are emerging to rescue it." Discuss with reference to India's role. (15 marks)
What are the limits of coalitions of the willing in reforming global governance? (10 marks)
"In international relations, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must." How can a rules-based order change this? (10 marks, GS4)

practice.q: "Multilateralism is under severe pressure, yet new coalitions are emerging to rescue it." Discuss with reference to India's role.

answer.t: In September 2026, India, the EU, Brazil, Canada, Kenya, Australia and Barbados co-sponsored the Partners for Multilateralism (P4M) at the 81st UNGA, just as the US, the system's founder, turns away from it.

pts.t: The US rejects institutions it built, in word and deed.
pts.ex: Withdrawals from the WHO and the Paris Agreement.

pts.t: Rules are flouted with frequency and impunity.
pts.ex: Wars in Europe and West Asia.

pts.t: Key bodies cannot act or reform.
pts.ex: WTO Appellate Body non-functional since 2019; UNSC reform stalled.

pts.t: Institutions reflect 1945, not today's balance of power.
Competing models of global governance divide states.
Institutions seem distant from the people they affect.
Mixed membership builds trust across old divides.
pts.ex: P4M joins large and small states of both.

pts.t: Commitment to cooperation that is open, fair, equitable and inclusive.
Small coalitions act faster than universal bodies.
Groupings amplify developing countries' demands.
pts.ex: BRICS; India's Voice of the Global South summits.

pts.t: Declarations without costed plans fade.
Without clarity, they overlap with rival initiatives.
Ignoring affected people breeds discontent.
Many small coalitions can weaken universal institutions.
India sits in the Quad, BRICS, SCO and P4M and can link rival blocs.
Push the South's agenda on finance, climate and technology.
pts.ex: African Union's G20 membership under India's 2023 presidency.

pts.t: Press for UNSC and WTO reform with like-minded partners.
Back P4M with concrete projects, costs and burden-sharing.
Bring civilisational ideas such as Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam and LiFE into global norms.
pts.ex: G20 theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future'.

pts.t: Keep commitments, as on climate targets met early.

answer.t: As great powers retreat, coalitions like P4M can keep multilateralism alive; India, as a bridging power, can help turn declarations into a fairer, workable order.

title: PM: India to add 500 GW non-fossil fuel capacity in the next 10-11 years
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Climate change; Investment models · GS2 › International agreements (Paris Agreement)
summary: At the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit, the PM set a goal of adding 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in 10–11 years, noting India met its Paris target of half its capacity from non-fossil sources five years early.
evolution: Editorial: E100 alone will not secure energy; diesel dominates oil demand.
Editorial page: energy security depends on electrification and how we do it.
PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity addition goal for the next decade.
ideas: Early delivery on Paris: India pledged that half its installed power capacity would be non-fossil and met it in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
GS2 · Paris Agreement / GS3 · Climate
Meeting the Paris non-fossil capacity target five years early strengthens India's credibility in climate negotiations.
A bigger next step: the PM announced 500 GW of new non-fossil capacity over the next 10–11 years, calling the target difficult but achievable.
GS3 · Energy transition
India's new 500 GW goal signals that the energy transition is moving from targets met to scale-up.
Clean energy as energy security: the PM said clean-energy investment helped India avert a worse energy crisis during the West Asia war.
GS3 · Energy security / GS2 · Foreign policy
Domestic clean power insulates India from fossil-fuel shocks abroad.
Investment drives the shift: the PM cited large flows into renewables over the past decade and big opportunities ahead.
GS3 · Investment
Sustained private investment is what turns renewable targets into installed capacity.
Capacity is not yet generation: a majority of installed capacity is non-fossil, but intermittent sources need storage, grids and flexible supply to deliver reliable power.
GS3 · Infrastructure
Installed capacity must be matched by storage and transmission to become reliable clean electricity.
keywords: Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC)
A country's climate pledge under the Paris Agreement
GS2 · International agreements
India's early achievement of its NDC capacity target shows climate action matching commitment.
Installed capacity vs generation
Plant size versus electricity actually produced
GS3 · Energy
Non-fossil sources lead in installed capacity but still trail in generation share.
Energy storage
Batteries and pumped hydro that store power for later
GS3 · Energy
Storage is the missing link that makes solar and wind reliable.
Energy sovereignty
Meeting energy needs from domestic sources
GS3 · Energy security
Renewables move India from import dependence towards energy sovereignty.
data: Installed non-fossil capacity, and its share of total installed capacity of 558.89 GW
India has 308 GW of non-fossil capacity, 55.1% of total installed capacity (CEA).
Year India met its Paris pledge of 50% installed capacity from non-fossil sources, five years early
PM, at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit, via IE
India met its 50% non-fossil capacity pledge in 2025, five years ahead of the 2030 target.
examples: Paris target met five years early
50% non-fossil installed capacity reached in 2025
GS2 · International agreements · GS3 · Climate · Essay
India meeting its Paris capacity target early shows a developing country leading by delivery, not just pledges.
Clean energy and the West Asia war
Renewables cushioned India from a worse energy crisis
GS1 · Globalisation · GS2 · Energy security · GS3 · Energy
The West Asia war showed that every solar panel at home is a hedge against shocks abroad.
pyqs: Meeting 50% of energy needs from renewables by 2030 and shifting subsidies.
Challenges for India's energy security and measures.
Energy independence through clean technology by 2047.
India's changing climate policy in international fora.
Status and targets of renewable energy.

trend.t: Renewable questions moved from status and targets (2016) and solar costs (2015, 2020) to whether India will meet 50% renewables by 2030 (2022) and energy independence through clean technology by 2047 (2025). In 2026 the frame became energy security with growth and sustainability.
trend.watch: Renewable targets and energy security now come almost every year. Prepare the Paris target met early, the next goals, and the challenges of storage and grids.

potential: "India's energy transition has moved from setting targets to building systems." Examine with reference to renewable energy. (15 marks)
What challenges must India overcome to add 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in the next decade? (10 marks)

practice.q: What challenges must India overcome to add 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in the next decade?

answer.t: India has 308 GW of non-fossil capacity, 55.1% of the total (CEA), and met its Paris capacity target in 2025; the PM now seeks 500 GW more in 10–11 years.

pts.t: Solar and wind need batteries and pumped hydro for evening and night demand.
Grids must carry power from resource-rich to demand centres.
Large projects face land acquisition and local resistance.
Cost of capital and discom finances.
Dependence on imported equipment.
Balancing variable supply with demand.
Mandates and incentives for batteries and pumped hydro.
Expand inter-state transmission.
Improve finances to sustain purchases.
Cut dependence on imports.

answer.t: Having met its Paris target early, India's next test is turning capacity into reliable, round-the-clock clean power.
